newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia cautious on '97 economy despite '96 triumph.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia cautious on '97 economy despite '96 triumph.

text.p: Malaysia said on Friday its economy would expand by eight percent in 1997, the 10th straight year of growth, but would face the cooling influence of tight monetary and fiscal policies introduced last year.
The central Bank Negara Malaysia said in its 1996 annual report that the biggest challenges for the economy are rising property prices, inflation pressures and a large currrent account deficit.

Responding to international concerns, Malaysia in 1996 reined in galloping economic growth to 8.2 percent from 9.5 percent in 1995, reduced the current account deficit to 13 billion ringgit ($5.2 billion) from 18.7 billion and kept the inflation rate checked at 3.5 percent, the central bank said.
But Malaysia cannot rest on its laurels because "our open economy leaves us always vulnerable to external developments," a Bank Negara official told reporters at a briefing.
"In the immediate term, of course, the potential for inflation remains because of rising costs. There is need to monitor closely...asset prices (to ensure they) do not become a destabilising factor.
"And we also need to ensure that credit and monetary growth do not become a source of instability," she said.

Over the medium term, Malaysia needs to further reduce its external imbalances, improve efficiency and international competitiveness and sustain a higher savings rate to fund economic growth, the central bank official said.
Bank Negara forecast that gross domestic product (GDP) will grow at 7.8-8.2 percent, depending on whether exports pick up.
"The downside risk to this forecast would be slower manufacturing growth if the external (export) sector recovery is slower than expected," the official said.

The report said slower exports growth -- particularly in the electronics sector which accounts for two-thirds of Malaysia's manufactured exports -- could also widen the current account deficit this year, now estimated at 14.8 billion ringgit.
The Bank said that to maintain growth and keep inflation below four percent, Bank Negara would continue its tight monetary policy, which means interest rates would remain at a relatively high level.
Malaysia's three-month benchmark rate already is 1.7 percentage points above rates in the U.S. and four percentage points higher than those in Singapore, it said.
But, inflation "could be higher if certain costs we have seen increase recently -- higher wages and utility rates -- are passed on to consumers," the official said.
Wages in the chronically labour-short economy rose by 11.5 percent in 1996. Telephone, electricity and toll road tariffs were all raised during the year.
Rising asset prices, particularly in the property sector, are another inflationary factor which would be closely watched, the central bank said.
Loans to the property sector, which accounted for nearly 30 percent of all lending by the banking system last year, remained a big source of worry for Bank Negara, the report said.
Bank lending has increasingly favoured the "less productive" activities of consumption, stock purchases and the property sector, it said.

The growth in credit kept the supply of money high, with the broad M3 measure expanding by 22.7 percent last year from a peak of 27 percent in April, 1996. The central bank said it needed to fall further.
"We would be more comfortable if it is below 20 percent, but we don't do monetary targetting," she said.
